CollegeHOF = 2055 }} '''John Albert Elway Jr.''' (born June 28, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire 16-year career as a [[quarterback]] with the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Following his playing career, he then spent 11 years with the Broncos in various front office positions, eventually being promoted to [[General manager (sports)|general manager]]. Elway and former backup quarterback and head coach [[Gary Kubiak]] are the only individuals to be associated with all three of the Broncos' Super Bowl wins. Elway is widely regarded as one of the best quarterbacks in the history of the sport.{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Elliot |date=July 2, 2019 |title=Top 25 quarterbacks of all time: Patriots' Tom |website=Audacy |language=en}} At the time of his retirement in early 1999, Elway had the most victories by a starting quarterback and was statistically the second most prolific passer in NFL history.{{cite web | title=John Elway Calls It Quits | website=CBS News|agency=Associated Press | date=1999-05-02 | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/john-elway-calls-it-quits/ | access-date=2026-04-07}} He was also a prolific [[Rush (American and Canadian football)|rusher]] of the ball, being one of only two players to score a rushing touchdown in four different Super Bowls (the other being [[Thurman Thomas]]) and the only quarterback to do so.[http://www.nfl.com/superbowl/records/superbowls/player/passing "Super Bowl Records: Individual Passing"], NFL.com{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/super-bowl/leaders.htm |access-date=2024-06-15 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} While playing [[college football]] at [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]], Elway set several career records for passing attempts and completions and also received [[unanimous All-American]] honors. He was the first selection in the [[1983 NFL draft]], famously known as the "quarterback class of 1983", where he was taken by the [[1983 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]] before being traded to the Denver Broncos. In January 1987, Elway embarked on one of the most notable performances in sports and in NFL history, helping engineer a 98-yard, game-tying [[touchdown]] drive in the [[AFC Championship Game]] against the [[1986 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]], a moment later dubbed "[[The Drive (American football)|The Drive]]". Following that game in Cleveland, Elway and the Broncos lost in [[Super Bowl XXI]] to the [[1986 New York Giants season|New York Giants]]. After two more Super Bowl losses, the Broncos entered a period of decline; however, that ended during the [[1997 Denver Broncos season|1997 season]], as Elway and Denver won their first Super Bowl title in [[Super Bowl XXXII]]. The Broncos repeated as champions the [[1998 Denver Broncos season|following season]] in [[Super Bowl XXXIII]]. Elway was named MVP of that Super Bowl, which was the last game of his career, and in doing so Elway set a then-record five Super Bowl starts which was broken in February 2015 when [[Tom Brady]] of the [[New England Patriots]] started [[Super Bowl XLIX]]. After his retirement as a player, Elway served as general manager and executive vice president of football operations of the Broncos, which won four division titles, two AFC Championships, and [[Super Bowl 50]] during his tenure, making Elway a three-time Super Bowl Champion with the Broncos–two as a player and one as an executive. Elway was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2000 and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2004.

'''John E. Frank''' (born April 17, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1984 to 1988. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]]. Frank was selected by the 49ers in the second round of the [[1984 NFL draft]], and won two [[Super Bowl]]s with the team. After his football career, he became a hair restoration surgeon.

'''John Raymond Cappelletti''' (born August 9, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Los Angeles Rams]] and [[San Diego Chargers]].

He played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]], winning the [[Heisman Trophy]] in 1973.<ref name=cwhctrp>{{cite news |url=http://archives.chicagotribune.com/1973/12/05/page/93/article/cappelletti-wins-heisman-trophy |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |agency=UPI |title=Cappelletti wins Heisman Trophy |date=December 5, 1973 |page=1, sec. 3}}</ref><ref name=jcwhtrre>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=WwUrAAAAIBAJ&sjid=-pcFAAAAIBAJ&pg=6203%2C2498706 |newspaper=Reading Eagle |location=Pennsylvania |agency=Associated Press|title=John Cappelletti wins Heisman Trophy|date=December 4, 1973 |page=20}}</ref><ref name=cmthicem>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=X0oNAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BW0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7175%2C679444 |newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |last=Parascenzo |first=Marino |title=Heisman Trophy cometh to the Iceman - Cappelletti |date=December 5, 1973 |page=30}}</ref><ref name=chdbts>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=XAUrAAAAIBAJ&sjid=-pcFAAAAIBAJ&pg=6436%2C3420369 |newspaper=Reading Eagle |location=Pennsylvania |agency=Associated Press |title=Cappelletti had doubts Heisman Trophy |date=December 5, 1973 |page=68}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1993. Coach [[Joe Paterno]] said that Cappelletti was "the best football player I ever coached" or words to that effect.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=John Cappelletti, Pennsylvania Center for the Book |url=https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/bios/cappelletti__john#:~:text=Born%20in%20Pennsylvania%20on%20August,professional%20football%20for%20some%20years. |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=pabook.libraries.psu.edu}}</ref> Cappelletti's relationship with his younger brother Joey, who was stricken with [[leukemia]], was chronicled into a book and television movie, ''[[Something for Joey]]''.

'''John Joseph Fina''' (born March 11, 1969) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for 11 years in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), 10 of those with the [[Buffalo Bills]], and a one-year stint with the [[Arizona Cardinals]]. Fina attended [[Salpointe Catholic High School]] where he was first-team All-State his senior year, and is one of the several players in school history to have their jersey retired. Fina attended the [[University of Arizona]] where he was a brother of [[Sigma Phi Epsilon]]. '''John B. Corker''' (born December 29, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for four seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily for the [[Houston Oilers]]. He also played eight seasons in the [[Arena Football League]] (AFL). In 2002, Corker was elected into the [[Arena Football League Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.arenafootball.com/hallfame/ |title=Hall of Fame |publisher=Arena Football League |work=www.arenafootball.com |access-date=February 12, 2013 |archive-date=May 1, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160501030107/http://www.arenafootball.com/hallfame/ |url-status=usurped }}</ref>

Corker was named Big-8 Defensive Player of the Year in 1978 despite playing in only 7 games prior to tearing ligaments in his knee.  He returned in 1979 and was 2nd team All Big-8 and All-American.

He also played with the [[Michigan Panthers]] and the [[Memphis Showboats]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). Corker graduated from [[South Miami High School]] in 1976 ([[South Miami, Florida]],) where he played [[High school football|football]] and [[basketball]].

Corker was named USFL Defensive Player of the Year in 1983 after recording 28.5 sacks in 18 games while playing with the Michigan Panthers.  Corker's efforts also led the Panthers to the USFL Championship that same season.

After the Panthers merged with the Oakland Invaders before the 1985 USFL season, Corker signed with the Memphis Showboats.  One of his defensive mates was future NFL Hall of Famer, [[Reggie White]].  Corker finished his 3-year USFL career with 42 sacks in 54 games.

In 1994 Corker resurfaced with the Arena Football League's [[Miami Hooters]] playing 7 games for head coach Don Strock.

'''John Williams Fletcher''' (born August 22, 1965) is an American former [[Gridiron football|football]] [[offensive lineman|offensive]] and [[defensive lineman]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Texas A&I Javelinas football|Texas A&I Javelinas]] and later was a member of nine teams in four leagues; he played three games for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) in 1987 as a [[replacement player]].<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |title=John Fletcher stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FletJo20.htm |access-date=February 22, 2024 |publisher=Pro Football Reference}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=John Fletcher, G |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/john-fletcher/ |access-date=February 22, 2024 |work=NFL.com}}</ref>

Fletcher attended [[Foy H. Moody High School]] where he was used as a blocking [[tight end]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-times/141860989/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 20, 1982|page=19|title=Big John erases all doubt for the Trojans|author=Rowin, Dwight}} {{Open access}}</ref> He also played basketball and threw shot put for the track and field team, being named the school's best athlete.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141861179/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=July 8, 1987|page=26|title=290-pound Fletcher makes an impression|author=Tagliabue, Emil}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref name="auto3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141861299/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=March 13, 1983|page=57|title=Javelinas sign Fletcher}} {{Open access}}</ref> He committed to play [[college football]] at [[Texas A&I University]].<ref name="auto3"/> He played three years for the team as an [[offensive lineman]].<ref name="auto1"/>

After going unselected in the [[1987 NFL draft]], Fletcher was signed by the [[Cleveland Browns]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] and was moved to [[defensive lineman]], but did not make the team.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141861579/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 23, 1987|page=26|title=South Texas pros join picket lines|author=Tagliabue, Emil}} {{Open access}}</ref> He signed with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] as a [[replacement player]] during the [[1987 NFL strike]] and played three games as a backup [[offensive guard]].<ref name="auto2"/> He signed with the [[San Diego Chargers]] as a defensive lineman in 1988 but did not make the team.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141861793/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=February 19, 1988|page=21|title=A&I, Moody-ex Fletcher signs with Chargers as free agent|author=Tagliabue, Emil}} {{Open access}}</ref> He joined the [[New York Jets]] in 1989 but was released following a failed physical.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/press-and-sun-bulletin/141862057/|newspaper=[[Press and Sun Bulletin]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=May 16, 1989|page=21|title=Jets' camp intensifies in early going|agency=[[Associated Press]]}} {{Open access}}</ref>

Fletcher moved to the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) in 1990, spending time with both the [[Toronto Argonauts]] and [[Winnipeg Blue Bombers]] as a defensive lineman.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141862183/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=April 27, 1990|page=33|title=Bucs sign A&I's Blackmon}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141862303/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=February 25, 1991|page=41|title=WLAF opens new chapter for Moody's Fletcher|author=Tagliabue, Emil}} {{Open access}}</ref> He was selected by the [[Montreal Machine]] of the [[World League of American Football]] (WLAF) in 1991 and after being waived by them before the season, joined the [[San Antonio Riders]] and played eight games that year on defense, totaling a [[Quarterback sack|sack]].<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corpus-christi-caller-times/141862549/|newspaper=[[Corpus Christi Caller-Times]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=March 21, 1991|page=31|title=Fletcher with Riders}} {{Open access}}</ref><ref name="auto4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.statscrew.com/football/stats/p-fletcjoh001|website=StatsCrew.com|title=John Fletcher}}</ref> From 1992 to 1993, he then played in the [[Arena Football League]] (AFL) for the [[Cleveland Thunderbolts]] to finish his career.<ref name="auto4"/>
